blocks.text_en: 3.2.2. Architecture View Creation Process
blocks.html: 3.2.2. Architecture View Creation Process

section_path.title_en: 3.2. Developing Architecture Views in the ADM

blocks.text_en:
As mentioned above, the TOGAF framework encourages but does not mandate the use of ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022. The following description therefore covers both the situation where ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022 has been adopted
and where it has not.
blocks.html: As mentioned above, the TOGAF framework encourages but does not mandate the use of ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022. The following description therefore covers both the situation where ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022 has been adopted and where it has not.

section_path.title_en: 3.2. Developing Architecture Views in the ADM

blocks.text_en:
ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022 itself does not require any specific process for developing architecture viewpoints or creating views from them. Where
ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022 has been adopted and become well-established
practice within an organization, it will often be possible to create the required views for a particular architecture by following these steps:
blocks.html: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022 itself does not require any specific process for developing architecture viewpoints or creating views from them. Where ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022 has been adopted and become well-established practice within an organization, it will often be possible to create the required views for a particular architecture by following these steps:

section_path.title_en: 3.2. Developing Architecture Views in the ADM

blocks.text_en:
Refer to an existing library of architecture viewpoints Select the appropriate architecture viewpoints (based on the
stakeholders and concerns that need to be covered by views) Generate views of the system by using the selected architecture
viewpoints as templates
blocks.html:
1. Refer to an existing library of architecture viewpoints

  2. Select the appropriate architecture viewpoints (based on the stakeholders and concerns that need to be covered by views)

  3. Generate views of the system by using the selected architecture viewpoints as templates

section_path.title_en: 3.2. Developing Architecture Views in the ADM

blocks.text_en: This approach can be expected to bring the following benefits:
blocks.html: This approach can be expected to bring the following benefits:

section_path.title_en: 3.2. Developing Architecture Views in the ADM

blocks.text_en:
Less work for the architects (the architecture viewpoints have
already been defined and therefore the views can be created faster) Better comprehensibility for stakeholders (the architecture
viewpoints are already familiar) Greater confidence in the validity of the views (their
architecture viewpoints have a known track record)
blocks.html:
• Less work for the architects (the architecture viewpoints have already been defined and therefore the views can be created faster)

  • Better comprehensibility for stakeholders (the architecture viewpoints are already familiar)

  • Greater confidence in the validity of the views (their architecture viewpoints have a known track record)

section_path.title_en: 3.2. Developing Architecture Views in the ADM

blocks.text_en:
However, situations can always arise in which an architecture view is needed for which no appropriate architecture viewpoint has been predefined. This is also the situation, of course, when an organization has not yet incorporated ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022 into its architecture
practice and established a library of architecture viewpoints.
blocks.html: However, situations can always arise in which an architecture view is needed for which no appropriate architecture viewpoint has been predefined. This is also the situation, of course, when an organization has not yet incorporated ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022 into its architecture practice and established a library of architecture viewpoints.

section_path.title_en: 3.2. Developing Architecture Views in the ADM

blocks.text_en:
In each case, the architect may choose to develop a new architecture viewpoint that will cover the outstanding need, and then generate an architecture view from it. (This is ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022 recommended practice.) Alternatively, a more pragmatic approach can be equally successful: the architect can create an ad hoc architecture view for a specific system and later consider whether a generalized form of the
implicit architecture viewpoint should be defined explicitly and saved in a library, so that it can be re-used. (This is one way of
establishing a library of architecture viewpoints initially.)
blocks.html: In each case, the architect may choose to develop a new architecture viewpoint that will cover the outstanding need, and then generate an architecture view from it. (This is ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022 recommended practice.) Alternatively, a more pragmatic approach can be equally successful: the architect can create an ad hoc architecture view for a specific system and later consider whether a generalized form of the implicit architecture viewpoint should be defined explicitly and saved in a library, so that it can be re-used. (This is one way of establishing a library of architecture viewpoints initially.)

section_path.title_en: 3.2. Developing Architecture Views in the ADM

blocks.text_en:
Whatever the context, the architect should be aware that every architecture view has an architecture viewpoint, at least implicitly, and that defining the architecture viewpoint in a systematic way (as recommended by ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022) will help in assessing its effectiveness; i.e., does the architecture viewpoint cover the relevant
stakeholder concerns?
blocks.html: Whatever the context, the architect should be aware that every architecture view has an architecture viewpoint, at least implicitly, and that defining the architecture viewpoint in a systematic way (as recommended by ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022) will help in assessing its effectiveness; i.e., does the architecture viewpoint cover the relevant stakeholder concerns?

blocks.text_en: 3.3. Views, Tools, and Languages
blocks.html: 3.3. Views, Tools, and Languages

blocks.text_en:
The need for architecture views, and the process of developing them
following the ADM, is explained above. This section describes the
relationships between architecture views, the tools used to develop and analyze them, and a standard language enabling interoperability between the tools.
blocks.html: The need for architecture views, and the process of developing them following the ADM, is explained above. This section describes the relationships between architecture views, the tools used to develop and analyze them, and a standard language enabling interoperability between the tools.

blocks.text_en: 3.3.1. Overview

In order to achieve the goals of completeness and integrity in an
architecture, architecture views are usually developed, visualized,
communicated, and managed using a tool.
blocks.html: In order to achieve the goals of completeness and integrity in an architecture, architecture views are usually developed, visualized, communicated, and managed using a tool.

blocks.text_en:
In the current state of the market, different tools normally have to be used to develop and analyze different views of the architecture. It is highly desirable that an Architecture Description be encoded in a
standard language, to enable a standard approach to the description of architecture semantics and their re-use among different tools.
blocks.html: In the current state of the market, different tools normally have to be used to develop and analyze different views of the architecture. It is highly desirable that an Architecture Description be encoded in a standard language, to enable a standard approach to the description of architecture semantics and their re-use among different tools.

blocks.text_en:
An architecture viewpoint is also normally developed, visualized,
communicated, and managed using a tool, and it is also highly desirable that standard architecture viewpoints (i.e., templates or schemas) be
developed, so that different tools that deal in the same views can
interoperate, the fundamental elements of an architecture can be
re-used, and the Architecture Description can be shared among tools.
blocks.html: An architecture viewpoint is also normally developed, visualized, communicated, and managed using a tool, and it is also highly desirable that standard architecture viewpoints (i.e., templates or schemas) be developed, so that different tools that deal in the same views can interoperate, the fundamental elements of an architecture can be re-used, and the Architecture Description can be shared among tools.

blocks.text_en:
Issues relating to the evaluation of tools for architecture work are
discussed in detail in the TOGAF Standard — Architecture Development Method .
blocks.html: Issues relating to the evaluation of tools for architecture work are discussed in detail in the TOGAF Standard — Architecture Development Method.

blocks.text_en: 3.4. Architecture Views and Architecture Viewpoints
blocks.html: 3.4. Architecture Views and Architecture Viewpoints

section_path.title_en: 3.4.1. Example of Architecture Views and Architecture Viewpoints

blocks.text_en: 3.4.1. Example of Architecture Views and Architecture Viewpoints
blocks.html: 3.4.1. Example of Architecture Views and Architecture Viewpoints

section_path.title_en: 3.4.1. Example of Architecture Views and Architecture Viewpoints

blocks.text_en:
To illustrate the concepts of architecture views and architecture
viewpoints, consider the example of a very simple airport system with two different stakeholders: the pilot and the air traffic controller.
blocks.html: To illustrate the concepts of architecture views and architecture viewpoints, consider the example of a very simple airport system with two different stakeholders: the pilot and the air traffic controller.

section_path.title_en: 3.4.1. Example of Architecture Views and Architecture Viewpoints

blocks.text_en:
One architecture view can be developed from the architecture viewpoint of the pilot, which addresses the pilot’s concerns. Equally, another architecture view can be developed from the architecture viewpoint of
the air traffic controller. Neither architecture view completely describes the system in its entirety, because the architecture viewpoint of each stakeholder constrains (and reduces) how each sees the overall
system.
blocks.html: One architecture view can be developed from the architecture viewpoint of the pilot, which addresses the pilot’s concerns. Equally, another architecture view can be developed from the architecture viewpoint of the air traffic controller. Neither architecture view completely describes the system in its entirety, because the architecture viewpoint of each stakeholder constrains (and reduces) how each sees the overall system.

section_path.title_en: 3.4.1. Example of Architecture Views and Architecture Viewpoints

blocks.text_en:
The architecture viewpoint of the pilot comprises some concerns that are not relevant to the controller, such as passengers and fuel, while the architecture viewpoint of the controller comprises some concerns not
relevant to the pilot, such as other planes. There are also elements shared between the two architecture viewpoints, such as the communication model between the pilot and the controller, and the vital information about the plane itself.
blocks.html: The architecture viewpoint of the pilot comprises some concerns that are not relevant to the controller, such as passengers and fuel, while the architecture viewpoint of the controller comprises some concerns not relevant to the pilot, such as other planes. There are also elements shared between the two architecture viewpoints, such as the communication model between the pilot and the controller, and the vital information about the plane itself.

section_path.title_en: 3.4.1. Example of Architecture Views and Architecture Viewpoints

blocks.text_en: An architecture viewpoint is a model (or description) of the information contained in a view. In our example, one architecture viewpoint is the description of how the pilot sees the system, and the other architecture viewpoint is how the controller sees the system.
blocks.html: An architecture viewpoint is a model (or description) of the information contained in a view. In our example, one architecture viewpoint is the description of how the pilot sees the system, and the other architecture viewpoint is how the controller sees the system.

section_path.title_en: 3.4.1. Example of Architecture Views and Architecture Viewpoints

blocks.text_en:
Pilots describe the system from their perspective, using a model of
their position and vector toward or away from the runway. All pilots use this model, and the model has a specific language that is used to capture information and populate the model.
blocks.html: Pilots describe the system from their perspective, using a model of their position and vector toward or away from the runway. All pilots use this model, and the model has a specific language that is used to capture information and populate the model.

section_path.title_en: 3.4.1. Example of Architecture Views and Architecture Viewpoints

blocks.text_en:
Controllers describe the system differently, using a model of the
airspace and the locations and vectors of aircraft within the airspace. Again, all controllers use a common language derived from the common model in order to capture and communicate information pertinent to their
architecture viewpoint.
blocks.html: Controllers describe the system differently, using a model of the airspace and the locations and vectors of aircraft within the airspace. Again, all controllers use a common language derived from the common model in order to capture and communicate information pertinent to their architecture viewpoint.

section_path.title_en: 3.4.1. Example of Architecture Views and Architecture Viewpoints

blocks.text_en:
Fortunately, when controllers talk with pilots, they use a common
communication language. (In other words, the models representing their individual architecture viewpoints partially intersect.) Part of this common language is about location and vectors of aircraft, and is essential to safety.
blocks.html: Fortunately, when controllers talk with pilots, they use a common communication language. (In other words, the models representing their individual architecture viewpoints partially intersect.) Part of this common language is about location and vectors of aircraft, and is essential to safety.

section_path.title_en: 3.4.1. Example of Architecture Views and Architecture Viewpoints

blocks.text_en: So, in essence, each architecture viewpoint is an abstract model of how all the stakeholders of a particular type — all pilots, or all controllers — view the airport system.
blocks.html: So, in essence, each architecture viewpoint is an abstract model of how all the stakeholders of a particular type — all pilots, or all controllers — view the airport system.

section_path.title_en: 3.4.1. Example of Architecture Views and Architecture Viewpoints

blocks.text_en:
Tools exist to assist stakeholders, especially when they are interacting with complex models such as the model of an airspace, or the model of
air flight.
blocks.html: Tools exist to assist stakeholders, especially when they are interacting with complex models such as the model of an airspace, or the model of air flight.

section_path.title_en: 3.4.1. Example of Architecture Views and Architecture Viewpoints

blocks.text_en:
The interface to the human user of a tool is typically close to the
model and language associated with the architecture viewpoint. The
unique tools of the pilot are fuel, altitude, speed, and location
indicators. The main tool of the controller is radar. The common tool is a radio.
blocks.html: The interface to the human user of a tool is typically close to the model and language associated with the architecture viewpoint. The unique tools of the pilot are fuel, altitude, speed, and location indicators. The main tool of the controller is radar. The common tool is a radio.

section_path.title_en: 3.4.1. Example of Architecture Views and Architecture Viewpoints

blocks.text_en:
To summarize from the above example, we can see that an architecture view can subset the system through the perspective of the stakeholder, such as the pilot versus the controller. This subset can be described by an abstract model called an architecture viewpoint, such as an air flight versus an air space model. This description of the architecture view is documented in a partially specialized language, such as “pilot-speak” versus “controller-speak”. Tools are used to assist the stakeholders, and they interface with each other in terms of the
language derived from the architecture viewpoint (“pilot-speak” versus “controller-speak”).
blocks.html: To summarize from the above example, we can see that an architecture view can subset the system through the perspective of the stakeholder, such as the pilot versus the controller. This subset can be described by an abstract model called an architecture viewpoint, such as an air flight versus an air space model. This description of the architecture view is documented in a partially specialized language, such as “pilot-speak” versus “controller-speak”. Tools are used to assist the stakeholders, and they interface with each other in terms of the language derived from the architecture viewpoint (“pilot-speak” versus “controller-speak”).

section_path.title_en: 3.4.1. Example of Architecture Views and Architecture Viewpoints

blocks.text_en:
When stakeholders use common tools, such as the radio contact between
pilot and controller, a common language is essential.
blocks.html: When stakeholders use common tools, such as the radio contact between pilot and controller, a common language is essential.

section_path.title_en: 3.4.2. Architecture Views and Architecture Viewpoints in Enterprise Architecture

blocks.text_en: 3.4.2. Architecture Views and Architecture Viewpoints in Enterprise Architecture
blocks.html: 3.4.2. Architecture Views and Architecture Viewpoints in Enterprise Architecture

section_path.title_en: 3.4.2. Architecture Views and Architecture Viewpoints in Enterprise Architecture

blocks.text_en:
Now let us map this example to the Enterprise Architecture. Consider two
stakeholders in a new small computing system: the users and the
developers.
blocks.html: Now let us map this example to the Enterprise Architecture. Consider two stakeholders in a new small computing system: the users and the developers.

section_path.title_en: 3.4.2. Architecture Views and Architecture Viewpoints in Enterprise Architecture

blocks.text_en:
The users of the system have an architecture viewpoint that reflects
their concerns when interacting with the system, and the developers of
the system have a different architecture viewpoint. Architecture views
that are developed to address either of the two architecture viewpoints
are unlikely to exhaustively describe the whole system, because each
perspective reduces how each sees the system.
blocks.html: The users of the system have an architecture viewpoint that reflects their concerns when interacting with the system, and the developers of the system have a different architecture viewpoint. Architecture views that are developed to address either of the two architecture viewpoints are unlikely to exhaustively describe the whole system, because each perspective reduces how each sees the system.

section_path.title_en: 3.4.2. Architecture Views and Architecture Viewpoints in Enterprise Architecture

blocks.text_en:
The architecture viewpoint of the user is comprised of all the ways in
which the user interacts with the system, not seeing any details such as applications or Database Management Systems (DBMS).
blocks.html: The architecture viewpoint of the user is comprised of all the ways in which the user interacts with the system, not seeing any details such as applications or Database Management Systems (DBMS).

section_path.title_en: 3.4.2. Architecture Views and Architecture Viewpoints in Enterprise Architecture

blocks.text_en:
The architecture viewpoint of the developer is one of productivity and
tools, and doesn’t include things such as actual live data and
connections with consumers.
blocks.html: The architecture viewpoint of the developer is one of productivity and tools, and doesn’t include things such as actual live data and connections with consumers.

section_path.title_en: 3.4.2. Architecture Views and Architecture Viewpoints in Enterprise Architecture

blocks.text_en:
However, there are things that are shared, such as descriptions of the
processes that are enabled by the system and/or communications protocols set up for users to communicate problems directly to development.
blocks.html: However, there are things that are shared, such as descriptions of the processes that are enabled by the system and/or communications protocols set up for users to communicate problems directly to development.

section_path.title_en: 3.4.2. Architecture Views and Architecture Viewpoints in Enterprise Architecture

blocks.text_en:
In this example, one architecture viewpoint is the description of how
the user sees the system, and the other architecture viewpoint is how
the developer sees the system. Users describe the system from their
perspective, using a model of availability, response time, and access to information. All users of the system use this model, and the model has a specific language.
blocks.html: In this example, one architecture viewpoint is the description of how the user sees the system, and the other architecture viewpoint is how the developer sees the system. Users describe the system from their perspective, using a model of availability, response time, and access to information. All users of the system use this model, and the model has a specific language.

section_path.title_en: 3.4.2. Architecture Views and Architecture Viewpoints in Enterprise Architecture

blocks.text_en: Developers describe the system differently than users, using a model of software connected to hardware distributed over a network, etc. However, there are many types of developers (database, security, etc.) of the system, and they do not have a common language derived from the model.
blocks.html: Developers describe the system differently than users, using a model of software connected to hardware distributed over a network, etc. However, there are many types of developers (database, security, etc.) of the system, and they do not have a common language derived from the model.

section_path.title_en: 3.4.3. Need for a Common Language and Interoperable Tools for Architecture Description

blocks.text_en: 3.4.3. Need for a Common Language and Interoperable Tools for Architecture Description
blocks.html: 3.4.3. Need for a Common Language and Interoperable Tools for Architecture Description

section_path.title_en: 3.4.3. Need for a Common Language and Interoperable Tools for Architecture Description

blocks.text_en:
Tools exist for both users and developers. Tools such as online help are there specifically for users, and attempt to use the language of the user. Many different tools exist for different types of developers, but they suffer from the lack of a common language that is required to bring
the system together. It is difficult, if not impossible, in the current state of the tools market to have one tool interoperate with another
tool.

Many different tools exist for different types of developers, but they suffer from the lack of a common language that is required to bring the system together. It is difficult, if not impossible, in the current state of the tools market to have one tool interoperate with another tool.

blocks.text_en: 3.5. Conclusions
blocks.html: 3.5. Conclusions

blocks.text_en:
This section attempts to deal with views in a structured manner, but
this is by no means a complete treatise on views.
blocks.html: This section attempts to deal with views in a structured manner, but this is by no means a complete treatise on views.

blocks.text_en: In general, the TOGAF framework embraces the concepts and definitions presented in ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022, specifically the concepts that help guide the development of an architecture view and make the architecture view actionable. These concepts can be summarized as:

blocks.text_en:
Selecting a key stakeholder Understanding their concerns and generalizing/documenting those
concerns Understanding how to model and deal with those concerns

blocks.text_en: 3.6. Architectural Artifacts by ADM Phase
blocks.html: 3.6. Architectural Artifacts by ADM Phase

blocks.text_en: 3.6.1. Catalog, Matrix, and Diagram Concept
blocks.html: 3.6.1. Catalog, Matrix, and Diagram Concept

blocks.text_en:
The Enterprise Metamodel is used as a technique to structure
architectural information in an ordered way so that it can be processed to meet the stakeholder needs. The majority of architecture stakeholders do not actually need to know what the architecture metamodel is and are
only concerned with specific issues, such as “what functionality does this application support?”, “which processes will be impacted by this project?”, etc. In order to meet the needs of these stakeholders, the TOGAF concepts of building blocks, catalogs, matrices, and diagrams are used.
blocks.html: The Enterprise Metamodel is used as a technique to structure architectural information in an ordered way so that it can be processed to meet the stakeholder needs. The majority of architecture stakeholders do not actually need to know what the architecture metamodel is and are only concerned with specific issues, such as “what functionality does this application support?”, “which processes will be impacted by this project?”, etc. In order to meet the needs of these stakeholders, the TOGAF concepts of building blocks, catalogs, matrices, and diagrams are used.

blocks.text_en:
Building blocks are entities of a particular type within the metamodel
(for example, a business service called “Purchase Order”). Building
blocks carry metadata according to the metamodel, which supports query
and analysis. For example, business services have a metadata attribute
for owner, which allows a stakeholder to query all business services owned by a particular organization. Building blocks may also include
dependent or contained entities as appropriate to the context of the
architecture (for example, a business service called “Purchase Order” may implicitly include a number of processes, data entities, application components, etc.).
blocks.html: Building blocks are entities of a particular type within the metamodel (for example, a business service called “Purchase Order”). Building blocks carry metadata according to the metamodel, which supports query and analysis. For example, business services have a metadata attribute for owner, which allows a stakeholder to query all business services owned by a particular organization. Building blocks may also include dependent or contained entities as appropriate to the context of the architecture (for example, a business service called “Purchase Order” may implicitly include a number of processes, data entities, application components, etc.).

blocks.text_en:
Catalogs are lists of building blocks of a specific type, or of related types, that are used for governance or reference purposes (for example, an organization chart, showing locations and actors). As with building
blocks, catalogs carry metadata according to the metamodel, which
supports query and analysis.
blocks.html: Catalogs are lists of building blocks of a specific type, or of related types, that are used for governance or reference purposes (for example, an organization chart, showing locations and actors). As with building blocks, catalogs carry metadata according to the metamodel, which supports query and analysis.

blocks.text_en:
Matrices are grids that show relationships between two or more model entities. Matrices are used to represent relationships that are
list-based rather than graphical in their usage (for example, a CRUD matrix showing which applications Create, Read, Update, and Delete a particular type of data is difficult to represent visually).
blocks.html: Matrices are grids that show relationships between two or more model entities. Matrices are used to represent relationships that are list-based rather than graphical in their usage (for example, a CRUD matrix showing which applications Create, Read, Update, and Delete a particular type of data is difficult to represent visually).

blocks.text_en:
Diagrams are renderings of architectural content in a graphical format to allow stakeholders to retrieve the required information. Diagrams can
also be used as a technique for graphically populating architecture
content or for checking the completeness of information that has been collected. The TOGAF Content Framework defines a set of architecture diagrams to be created (e.g., organization chart). Each of these diagrams may be created several times for an architecture with different
style or content coverage to suit stakeholder concerns.
blocks.html: Diagrams are renderings of architectural content in a graphical format to allow stakeholders to retrieve the required information. Diagrams can also be used as a technique for graphically populating architecture content or for checking the completeness of information that has been collected. The TOGAF Content Framework defines a set of architecture diagrams to be created (e.g., organization chart). Each of these diagrams may be created several times for an architecture with different style or content coverage to suit stakeholder concerns.

blocks.text_en:
Building blocks, catalogs, matrices, and diagrams are all concepts that are well supported by leading Enterprise Architecture tools. In environments where tools are used to model the architecture, such tools
typically support mechanisms to search, filter, and query the
Architecture Repository.
blocks.html: Building blocks, catalogs, matrices, and diagrams are all concepts that are well supported by leading Enterprise Architecture tools. In environments where tools are used to model the architecture, such tools typically support mechanisms to search, filter, and query the Architecture Repository.

blocks.text_en:
On-demand querying of the Architecture Repository (such as the business service ownership example mentioned above) can be used to generate ad hoc catalogs, matrices, and diagrams of the architecture. As this type
of query is by nature required to be flexible, it is therefore not
restricted or defined within the Enterprise Metamodel.
blocks.html: On-demand querying of the Architecture Repository (such as the business service ownership example mentioned above) can be used to generate ad hoc catalogs, matrices, and diagrams of the architecture. As this type of query is by nature required to be flexible, it is therefore not restricted or defined within the Enterprise Metamodel.

with the TOGAF Enterprise Metamodel.

blocks.text_en: 3.6.2. Preliminary Phase
blocks.html: 3.6.2. Preliminary Phase

blocks.text_en:
The following describes catalogs, matrices, and diagrams that may be
created within the Preliminary Phase, as described in the TOGAF Standard — Architecture Development Method .
blocks.html: The following describes catalogs, matrices, and diagrams that may be created within the Preliminary Phase, as described in the TOGAF Standard — Architecture Development Method.

blocks.text_en: 3.6.2.1. Principles Catalog
blocks.html: 3.6.2.1. Principles Catalog

blocks.text_en:
The Principles catalog captures principles of the Business and
Architecture Principles that describe what a “good” solution or
architecture should look like. Principles are used to evaluate and agree an outcome for architecture decision points. Principles are also used as a tool to assist in architectural governance of change initiatives.
blocks.html: The Principles catalog captures principles of the Business and Architecture Principles that describe what a “good” solution or architecture should look like. Principles are used to evaluate and agree an outcome for architecture decision points. Principles are also used as a tool to assist in architectural governance of change initiatives.

blocks.text_en: 3.6.3. Phase A: Architecture Vision
blocks.html: 3.6.3. Phase A: Architecture Vision

blocks.text_en:
The following describes catalogs, matrices, and diagrams that may be
created within Phase A (Architecture Vision) as described in the TOGAF Standard — Architecture Development Method .
blocks.html: The following describes catalogs, matrices, and diagrams that may be created within Phase A (Architecture Vision) as described in the TOGAF Standard — Architecture Development Method.

blocks.text_en: 3.6.3.1. Stakeholder Catalog
blocks.html: 3.6.3.1. Stakeholder Catalog

blocks.text_en:
The purpose of the Stakeholder catalog is to identify the stakeholders for the architecture engagement, their influence over the engagement, and their key questions, issues, or concerns that must be addressed by
the architecture framework.
The Stakeholder catalog is referenced in creating a stakeholder map, showing which stakeholders are involved with a specific aspect of the Enterprise Architecture, their level of involvement, and their key concerns.
blocks.html: The purpose of the Stakeholder catalog is to identify the stakeholders for the architecture engagement, their influence over the engagement, and their key questions, issues, or concerns that must be addressed by the architecture framework. The Stakeholder catalog is referenced in creating a stakeholder map, showing which stakeholders are involved with a specific aspect of the Enterprise Architecture, their level of involvement, and their key concerns.

blocks.text_en: Understanding stakeholders and their requirements allows an architect to focus effort in areas that meet the needs of stakeholders (see the TOGAF Standard — ADM Techniques ).
blocks.html: Understanding stakeholders and their requirements allows an architect to focus effort in areas that meet the needs of stakeholders (see the TOGAF Standard — ADM Techniques).

blocks.text_en:
Due to the potentially sensitive nature of stakeholder mapping
information and the fact that the Architecture Vision phase is intended to be conducted using informal modeling techniques, no specific metamodel entities will be used to generate a Stakeholder catalog.
blocks.html: Due to the potentially sensitive nature of stakeholder mapping information and the fact that the Architecture Vision phase is intended to be conducted using informal modeling techniques, no specific metamodel entities will be used to generate a Stakeholder catalog.

blocks.text_en: 3.6.3.2. Value Chain Diagram
blocks.html: 3.6.3.2. Value Chain Diagram

blocks.text_en:
A Value Chain diagram provides a high-level orientation view of an
enterprise and how it interacts with the outside world. In contrast to the more formal organization map developed within Phase B (Business Architecture), the Value Chain diagram focuses on presentational impact.
blocks.html: A Value Chain diagram provides a high-level orientation view of an enterprise and how it interacts with the outside world. In contrast to the more formal organization map developed within Phase B (Business Architecture), the Value Chain diagram focuses on presentational impact.

blocks.text_en:
The purpose of this diagram is to quickly on-board and align
stakeholders for a particular change initiative, so that all
participants understand the high-level functional and organizational
context of the architecture engagement.
blocks.html: The purpose of this diagram is to quickly on-board and align stakeholders for a particular change initiative, so that all participants understand the high-level functional and organizational context of the architecture engagement.

blocks.text_en: 3.6.3.3. Solution Concept Diagram
blocks.html: 3.6.3.3. Solution Concept Diagram

blocks.text_en: A Solution Concept diagram provides a high-level orientation of the solution that is envisaged in order to meet the objectives of the architecture engagement. In contrast to the more formal and detailed architecture diagrams developed in the following phases, the solution concept represents a “pencil sketch” of the expected solution at the outset of the engagement.
blocks.html: A Solution Concept diagram provides a high-level orientation of the solution that is envisaged in order to meet the objectives of the architecture engagement. In contrast to the more formal and detailed architecture diagrams developed in the following phases, the solution concept represents a “pencil sketch” of the expected solution at the outset of the engagement.

blocks.text_en: This diagram may embody key objectives, requirements, and constraints for the engagement and also highlight work areas to be investigated in more detail with formal architecture modeling.
blocks.html: This diagram may embody key objectives, requirements, and constraints for the engagement and also highlight work areas to be investigated in more detail with formal architecture modeling.

blocks.text_en:
Its purpose is to quickly on-board and align stakeholders for a
particular change initiative, so that all participants understand what the architecture engagement is seeking to achieve and how it is expected that a particular solution approach will meet the needs of the enterprise.
blocks.html: Its purpose is to quickly on-board and align stakeholders for a particular change initiative, so that all participants understand what the architecture engagement is seeking to achieve and how it is expected that a particular solution approach will meet the needs of the enterprise.

blocks.text_en: 3.6.3.4. Business Model Diagram
blocks.html: 3.6.3.4. Business Model Diagram

blocks.text_en:
A model describing the rationale for how an enterprise creates,
delivers, and captures value.
blocks.html: A model describing the rationale for how an enterprise creates, delivers, and captures value.

blocks.text_en: 3.6.3.5. Business Capability Map
blocks.html: 3.6.3.5. Business Capability Map

blocks.text_en: A diagram that shows the business capabilities that an enterprise needs to meet its purposes.
blocks.html: A diagram that shows the business capabilities that an enterprise needs to meet its purposes.

blocks.text_en: 3.6.3.6. Value Stream Map
blocks.html: 3.6.3.6. Value Stream Map

blocks.text_en:
A diagram representing an end-to-end collection of value-adding
activities that create an overall result for a customer, stakeholder, or end user.
blocks.html: A diagram representing an end-to-end collection of value-adding activities that create an overall result for a customer, stakeholder, or end user.

blocks.text_en: 3.6.4. Phase B: Business Architecture
blocks.html: 3.6.4. Phase B: Business Architecture

blocks.text_en:
The following describes catalogs, matrices, and diagrams that may be
created within Phase B (Business Architecture) as described in the TOGAF Standard — Architecture Development Method .
blocks.html: The following describes catalogs, matrices, and diagrams that may be created within Phase B (Business Architecture) as described in the TOGAF Standard — Architecture Development Method.

blocks.text_en: 3.6.4.1. Organization/Actor Catalog
blocks.html: 3.6.4.1. Organization/Actor Catalog

blocks.text_en: The purpose of the Organization/Actor catalog is to capture a definitive listing of all participants that interact with IT, including users and owners of IT systems.
blocks.html: The purpose of the Organization/Actor catalog is to capture a definitive listing of all participants that interact with IT, including users and owners of IT systems.

blocks.text_en:
The Organization/Actor catalog can be referenced when developing
requirements in order to test for completeness.
blocks.html: The Organization/Actor catalog can be referenced when developing requirements in order to test for completeness.

blocks.text_en:
For example, requirements for an application that services customers can be tested for completeness by verifying exactly which customer types
need to be supported and whether there are any particular requirements or restrictions for user types.
blocks.html: For example, requirements for an application that services customers can be tested for completeness by verifying exactly which customer types need to be supported and whether there are any particular requirements or restrictions for user types.

The Organization/Actor catalog contains the following metamodel
entities:
blocks.html: The Organization/Actor catalog contains the following metamodel entities:

blocks.text_en:
Organization Unit Actor Location (may be included in this catalog if an independent Location
catalog is not maintained)
blocks.html:

  • Actor

  • Location (may be included in this catalog if an independent Location catalog is not maintained)

blocks.text_en: 3.6.4.2. Driver/Goal/Objective Catalog
blocks.html: 3.6.4.2. Driver/Goal/Objective Catalog

blocks.text_en:
The purpose of the Driver/Goal Objective catalog is to provide a
cross-organizational reference of how an organization meets its drivers in practical terms through goals, objectives, and (optionally) measures.
blocks.html: The purpose of the Driver/Goal Objective catalog is to provide a cross-organizational reference of how an organization meets its drivers in practical terms through goals, objectives, and (optionally) measures.

blocks.text_en:
Publishing a definitive breakdown of drivers, goals, and objectives
allows change initiatives within the enterprise to identify synergies across the organization (e.g., multiple organizations attempting to achieve similar objectives), which in turn allow stakeholders to be identified and related change initiatives to be aligned or consolidated.
blocks.html: Publishing a definitive breakdown of drivers, goals, and objectives allows change initiatives within the enterprise to identify synergies across the organization (e.g., multiple organizations attempting to achieve similar objectives), which in turn allow stakeholders to be identified and related change initiatives to be aligned or consolidated.

blocks.text_en:
The Driver/Goal/Objective catalog contains the following metamodel
entities:
blocks.html: The Driver/Goal/Objective catalog contains the following metamodel entities:

blocks.text_en: Organization Unit Driver Goal Objective Measure (may optionally be included)
blocks.html:
• Organization Unit

  • Driver

  • Goal

  • Objective

  • Measure (may optionally be included)

blocks.text_en: 3.6.4.3. Role Catalog

The purpose of the Role catalog is to provide a listing of all authorization levels or zones within an enterprise. Frequently, application security or behavior is defined against locally understood concepts of authorization that create complex and unexpected consequences when combined on the user desktop.
blocks.html: The purpose of the Role catalog is to provide a listing of all authorization levels or zones within an enterprise. Frequently, application security or behavior is defined against locally understood concepts of authorization that create complex and unexpected consequences when combined on the user desktop.

blocks.text_en:
If roles are defined, understood, and aligned across organizations and applications, this allows for a more seamless user experience and
generally more secure applications, as administrators do not need to resort to workarounds in order to enable users to carry out their jobs.
blocks.html: If roles are defined, understood, and aligned across organizations and applications, this allows for a more seamless user experience and generally more secure applications, as administrators do not need to resort to workarounds in order to enable users to carry out their jobs.

blocks.text_en:
In addition to supporting security definition for the enterprise, the
Role catalog also forms a key input to identifying organizational change management impacts, defining job functions, and executing end-user training.
blocks.html: In addition to supporting security definition for the enterprise, the Role catalog also forms a key input to identifying organizational change management impacts, defining job functions, and executing end-user training.

blocks.text_en:
As each role implies access to a number of business functions, if any of these business functions are impacted then change management will be required, organizational responsibilities may need to be redefined, and
retraining may be needed.
blocks.html: As each role implies access to a number of business functions, if any of these business functions are impacted then change management will be required, organizational responsibilities may need to be redefined, and retraining may be needed.

blocks.text_en: The Role catalog contains the following metamodel entities:
blocks.html: The Role catalog contains the following metamodel entities:

blocks.text_en: Role
blocks.html: • Role

blocks.text_en: 3.6.4.4. Business Service/Function Catalog
blocks.html: 3.6.4.4. Business Service/Function Catalog

blocks.text_en: The purpose of the Business Service/Function catalog is to provide a functional decomposition in a form that can be filtered, reported on, and queried, as a supplement to graphical Functional Decomposition diagrams.
blocks.html: The purpose of the Business Service/Function catalog is to provide a functional decomposition in a form that can be filtered, reported on, and queried, as a supplement to graphical Functional Decomposition diagrams.

blocks.text_en:
The Business Service/Function catalog can be used to identify
capabilities of an organization and to understand the level that
governance is applied to the functions of an organization. This
functional decomposition can be used to identify new capabilities
required to support business change or may be used to determine the scope of change initiatives, applications, or technology components.
blocks.html: The Business Service/Function catalog can be used to identify capabilities of an organization and to understand the level that governance is applied to the functions of an organization. This functional decomposition can be used to identify new capabilities required to support business change or may be used to determine the scope of change initiatives, applications, or technology components.

blocks.text_en: The Business Service/Function catalog contains the following metamodel entities:
blocks.html: The Business Service/Function catalog contains the following metamodel entities:

blocks.text_en: Organization Unit Business Function Business Service Application Service (may optionally be included here)
blocks.html:
• Organization Unit

  • Business Function

  • Business Service

  • Application Service (may optionally be included here)

blocks.text_en: 3.6.4.5. Location Catalog
blocks.html: 3.6.4.5. Location Catalog

blocks.text_en:
The Location catalog provides a listing of all locations where an
enterprise carries out business operations or houses architecturally
relevant assets, such as data centers or end-user computing equipment.
blocks.html: The Location catalog provides a listing of all locations where an enterprise carries out business operations or houses architecturally relevant assets, such as data centers or end-user computing equipment.

blocks.text_en:
Maintaining a definitive list of locations allows change initiatives to quickly define a location scope and to test for completeness when assessing current landscapes or proposed target solutions. For example,
a project to upgrade desktop operating systems will need to identify all locations where desktop operating systems are deployed.
blocks.html: Maintaining a definitive list of locations allows change initiatives to quickly define a location scope and to test for completeness when assessing current landscapes or proposed target solutions. For example, a project to upgrade desktop operating systems will need to identify all locations where desktop operating systems are deployed.

blocks.text_en: Similarly, when new systems are being implemented a diagram of locations is essential in order to develop appropriate deployment strategies that comprehend both user and application location and identify location-related issues, such as internationalization, localization, timezone impacts on availability, distance impacts on latency, network impacts on bandwidth, and access.
blocks.html: Similarly, when new systems are being implemented a diagram of locations is essential in order to develop appropriate deployment strategies that comprehend both user and application location and identify location-related issues, such as internationalization, localization, timezone impacts on availability, distance impacts on latency, network impacts on bandwidth, and access.

blocks.text_en: 3.6.4.6. Process/Event/Control/Product Catalog
blocks.html: 3.6.4.6. Process/Event/Control/Product Catalog

blocks.text_en:
The Process/Event/Control/Product catalog provides a hierarchy of processes, events that trigger processes, outputs from processes, and controls applied to the execution of processes. This catalog provides a
supplement to any Process Flow diagrams that are created and allows an enterprise to filter, report, and query across organizations and processes to identify scope, commonality, or impact.
blocks.html: The Process/Event/Control/Product catalog provides a hierarchy of processes, events that trigger processes, outputs from processes, and controls applied to the execution of processes. This catalog provides a supplement to any Process Flow diagrams that are created and allows an enterprise to filter, report, and query across organizations and processes to identify scope, commonality, or impact.

blocks.text_en:
For example, the Process/Event/Control/Product catalog allows an
enterprise to see relationships of processes to sub-processes in order
to identify the full chain of impacts resulting from changing a
high-level process.
blocks.html: For example, the Process/Event/Control/Product catalog allows an enterprise to see relationships of processes to sub-processes in order to identify the full chain of impacts resulting from changing a high-level process.

blocks.html: 3.6.4.7. Contract/Measure Catalog

blocks.text_en: The Contract/Measure catalog provides a listing of all agreed service contracts and the measures attached to those contracts. It forms the master list of service levels agreed to across the enterprise.
blocks.html: The Contract/Measure catalog provides a listing of all agreed service contracts and the measures attached to those contracts. It forms the master list of service levels agreed to across the enterprise.

blocks.html: 3.6.4.8. Business Capabilities Catalog

blocks.html: A listing of end-to-end collections of the different stages for the value-adding activities that create an overall result for customer, stakeholder, or end user.

blocks.text_en: 3.6.4.11. Business Glossary Catalog
blocks.html: 3.6.4.11. Business Glossary Catalog

blocks.text_en:
This catalog contains the name and unambiguous description of all
elements contained in or interacting with the Enterprise Architecture.
blocks.html: This catalog contains the name and unambiguous description of all elements contained in or interacting with the Enterprise Architecture.

blocks.text_en:
Optional information could include element enterprise synonyms,
abbreviations/acronyms, and relationships with other elements. This catalog provides the semantics to be used by all analysts (e.g., business, information, and system) for their architecture products,
including information/data models, and evolves throughout the ADM.

blocks.html: 3.6.4.12. Business Interaction Matrix

blocks.text_en:
The purpose of this matrix is to depict the relationship interactions
between organizations and business functions across the enterprise.
blocks.html: The purpose of this matrix is to depict the relationship interactions between organizations and business functions across the enterprise.

blocks.text_en:
Understanding business interaction of an enterprise is important as it
helps to highlight value chain and dependencies across organizations.
blocks.html: Understanding business interaction of an enterprise is important as it helps to highlight value chain and dependencies across organizations.

blocks.html: 3.6.4.13. Actor/Role Matrix

blocks.text_en: The purpose of this matrix is to show which actors perform which roles, supporting definition of security and skills requirements.

Understanding Actor-to-Role relationships is a key supporting tool in

blocks.text_en: 3.6.4.17. Business Footprint Diagram
blocks.html: 3.6.4.17. Business Footprint Diagram

blocks.text_en:
A Business Footprint diagram describes the links between business goals,
organizational units, business functions, and services, and maps these
functions to the technical components delivering the required
capability.
blocks.html: A Business Footprint diagram describes the links between business goals, organizational units, business functions, and services, and maps these functions to the technical components delivering the required capability.

blocks.text_en:
A Business Footprint diagram provides a clear traceability between a
technical component and the business goal that it satisfies, while also
demonstrating ownership of the services identified.
blocks.html: A Business Footprint diagram provides a clear traceability between a technical component and the business goal that it satisfies, while also demonstrating ownership of the services identified.

blocks.text_en:
A Business Footprint diagram demonstrates only the key facts linking
organization unit functions to delivery services and is utilized as a
communication platform for senior-level (CxO) stakeholders.
blocks.html: A Business Footprint diagram demonstrates only the key facts linking organization unit functions to delivery services and is utilized as a communication platform for senior-level (CxO) stakeholders.

blocks.text_en: 3.6.4.18. Business Service/Information Diagram
blocks.html: 3.6.4.18. Business Service/Information Diagram

blocks.text_en:
The Business Service/Information diagram shows the information needed to support one or more business services. The Business Service/Information diagram shows what data is consumed by or produced by a business service
and may also show the source of information.
blocks.html: The Business Service/Information diagram shows the information needed to support one or more business services. The Business Service/Information diagram shows what data is consumed by or produced by a business service and may also show the source of information.

blocks.text_en: The Business Service/Information diagram shows an initial representation of the information present within the architecture and therefore forms a basis for elaboration and refinement within Phase C (Data Architecture).
blocks.html: The Business Service/Information diagram shows an initial representation of the information present within the architecture and therefore forms a basis for elaboration and refinement within Phase C (Data Architecture).

blocks.text_en: 3.6.4.19. Functional Decomposition Diagram
blocks.html: 3.6.4.19. Functional Decomposition Diagram

blocks.text_en:
The purpose of the Functional Decomposition diagram is to show on a
single page the capabilities of an organization that are relevant to the
consideration of an architecture. By examining the capabilities of an
organization from a functional perspective, it is possible to quickly
develop models of what the organization does without being dragged into
extended debate on how the organization does it.
blocks.html: The purpose of the Functional Decomposition diagram is to show on a single page the capabilities of an organization that are relevant to the consideration of an architecture. By examining the capabilities of an organization from a functional perspective, it is possible to quickly develop models of what the organization does without being dragged into extended debate on how the organization does it.

blocks.text_en:
Once a basic Functional Decomposition diagram has been developed, it
becomes possible to layer heat maps on top of this diagram to show scope
and decisions. For example, the capabilities to be implemented in
different phases of a change program.
blocks.html: Once a basic Functional Decomposition diagram has been developed, it becomes possible to layer heat maps on top of this diagram to show scope and decisions. For example, the capabilities to be implemented in different phases of a change program.

blocks.text_en: 3.6.4.20. Product Lifecycle Diagram
blocks.html: 3.6.4.20. Product Lifecycle Diagram

blocks.text_en:
This diagram shows the possible state transitions of a business product,
from its creation or receipt to its sale, disposal, or destruction.
blocks.html: This diagram shows the possible state transitions of a business product, from its creation or receipt to its sale, disposal, or destruction.

blocks.text_en:
The product may be a product of any kind (physical, software, or
service).
blocks.html: The product may be a product of any kind (physical, software, or service).

blocks.text_en: 3.6.4.21. Goal/Objective/Business Service Diagram
blocks.html: 3.6.4.21. Goal/Objective/Business Service Diagram

blocks.text_en:
The purpose of a Goal/Objective/Business Service diagram is to define
the ways in which a business service contributes to the achievement of a
business vision or strategy.
blocks.html: The purpose of a Goal/Objective/Business Service diagram is to define the ways in which a business service contributes to the achievement of a business vision or strategy.

blocks.text_en:
Business services are associated with the drivers, goals, objectives,
and measures that they support, allowing the enterprise to understand
which business services contribute to similar aspects of business
performance. The Goal/Objective/Business Service diagram also provides
qualitative input on what constitutes high performance for a particular
business service.
blocks.html: Business services are associated with the drivers, goals, objectives, and measures that they support, allowing the enterprise to understand which business services contribute to similar aspects of business performance. The Goal/Objective/Business Service diagram also provides qualitative input on what constitutes high performance for a particular business service.

blocks.text_en: 3.6.4.22. Business Use-Case Diagram
blocks.html: 3.6.4.22. Business Use-Case Diagram

blocks.text_en:
A Business Use-Case diagram displays the relationships between consumers
and providers of business services. Business services are consumed by
actors or other business services and the Business Use-Case diagram
provides added richness in describing business capability by
illustrating how and when that capability is used.
blocks.html: A Business Use-Case diagram displays the relationships between consumers and providers of business services. Business services are consumed by actors or other business services and the Business Use-Case diagram provides added richness in describing business capability by illustrating how and when that capability is used.

blocks.text_en:
The purpose of the Business Use-Case diagram is to help to describe and
validate the interaction between actors and their roles to processes and
functions. As the architecture progresses, the use-case can evolve from
the business level to include data, application, and technology details.
Architectural business use-cases can also be re-used in systems design
work.
blocks.html: The purpose of the Business Use-Case diagram is to help to describe and validate the interaction between actors and their roles to processes and functions. As the architecture progresses, the use-case can evolve from the business level to include data, application, and technology details. Architectural business use-cases can also be re-used in systems design work.

blocks.text_en: 3.6.4.23. Organization Decomposition Diagram
blocks.html: 3.6.4.23. Organization Decomposition Diagram

blocks.text_en:
An Organization Decomposition diagram describes the links between actor,
roles, and location within an organization tree.
blocks.html: An Organization Decomposition diagram describes the links between actor, roles, and location within an organization tree.

blocks.text_en:
An organization map should provide a chain of command of owners and
decision-makers in the organization. Although it is not the intent of
the Organization Decomposition diagram to link goal to organization, it
should be possible to intuitively link the goals to the stakeholders
from the Organization Decomposition diagram.
blocks.html: An organization map should provide a chain of command of owners and decision-makers in the organization. Although it is not the intent of the Organization Decomposition diagram to link goal to organization, it should be possible to intuitively link the goals to the stakeholders from the Organization Decomposition diagram.

blocks.text_en: 3.6.4.24. Process Flow Diagram
blocks.html: 3.6.4.24. Process Flow Diagram

blocks.text_en:
The purpose of the Process Flow diagram is to depict all models and
mappings related to the process metamodel entity.
blocks.html: The purpose of the Process Flow diagram is to depict all models and mappings related to the process metamodel entity.

blocks.text_en:
Process Flow diagrams show sequential flow of control between activities
and may utilize swim-lane techniques to represent ownership and
realization of process steps. For example, the application that supports
a process step may be shown as a swim-lane.
blocks.html: Process Flow diagrams show sequential flow of control between activities and may utilize swim-lane techniques to represent ownership and realization of process steps. For example, the application that supports a process step may be shown as a swim-lane.

blocks.text_en:
In addition to showing a sequence of activity, process flows can also be
used to detail the controls that apply to a process, the events that
trigger or result from completion of a process, and also the products
that are generated from process execution.
blocks.html: In addition to showing a sequence of activity, process flows can also be used to detail the controls that apply to a process, the events that trigger or result from completion of a process, and also the products that are generated from process execution.

blocks.text_en:
Process Flow diagrams are useful in elaborating the architecture with
subject specialists, as they allow the specialist to describe “how the
job is done” for a particular function. Through this process, each
process step can become a more fine-grained function and can then in
turn be elaborated as a process.
blocks.html: Process Flow diagrams are useful in elaborating the architecture with subject specialists, as they allow the specialist to describe “how the job is done” for a particular function. Through this process, each process step can become a more fine-grained function and can then in turn be elaborated as a process.

blocks.text_en: 3.6.4.25. Business Event Diagram
blocks.html: 3.6.4.25. Business Event Diagram

blocks.text_en: The purpose of the Business Event diagram is to depict the relationship between events and process.
blocks.html: The purpose of the Business Event diagram is to depict the relationship between events and process.

blocks.text_en:
Certain events — such as arrival of certain information (e.g., customer
submits sales order) or a certain point in time (e.g., end of fiscal
quarter) — cause work and certain actions need to be undertaken within
the business. These are often referred to as “business events” or simply
“events” and are considered as triggers for a process. It is important
to note that the event has to trigger a process and generate a business
response or result.

These are often referred to as “business events” or simply “events” and are considered as triggers for a process. It is important to note that the event has to trigger a process and generate a business response or result.

blocks.text_en: 3.6.4.26. Business Capability Map
blocks.html: 3.6.4.26. Business Capability Map

blocks.text_en:
A diagram that shows the business capabilities that an enterprise needs
to meet its purposes.

blocks.html: 3.6.4.27. Value Stream Map

A diagram representing an end-to-end collection of value-adding
activities that create an overall result for a customer, stakeholder, or
end user.

blocks.text_en: 3.6.4.28. Organization Map
blocks.html: 3.6.4.28. Organization Map

blocks.text_en:
A diagram showing the relationships between the primary entities that
make up the enterprise, its partners, and stakeholders.
blocks.html: A diagram showing the relationships between the primary entities that make up the enterprise, its partners, and stakeholders.

blocks.text_en: 3.6.4.29. Information Map
blocks.html: 3.6.4.29. Information Map

blocks.text_en:
A collection of information concepts and their relationships to one
another. Information concepts, in effect, reflect the business
vocabulary; e.g., client, account, or product. Mapping information in
the Business Architecture starts with listing those elements that matter
most to the business as well as how they are described in business
terms.

Mapping information in the Business Architecture starts with listing those elements that matter most to the business as well as how they are described in business terms.

blocks.text_en: 3.6.5. Phase C: Data Architecture
blocks.html: 3.6.5. Phase C: Data Architecture

blocks.text_en:
The following describes catalogs, matrices, and diagrams that may be
created within Phase C (Data Architecture) as described in the TOGAF Standard — Architecture Development Method .
blocks.html: The following describes catalogs, matrices, and diagrams that may be created within Phase C (Data Architecture) as described in the TOGAF Standard — Architecture Development Method.

blocks.text_en: 3.6.5.1. Data Entity/Data Component Catalog
blocks.html: 3.6.5.1. Data Entity/Data Component Catalog

blocks.text_en:
This catalog identifies and maintains a list of the data used across the
enterprise, relating data entities to data components showing how data
entities are structured.
blocks.html: This catalog identifies and maintains a list of the data used across the enterprise, relating data entities to data components showing how data entities are structured.

blocks.text_en: Its purpose is to:
blocks.html: Its purpose is to:

blocks.text_en: Identify all data used in the enterprise Encourage effective data use

blocks.text_en: 3.6.5.2. Data Entity/Business Function Matrix
blocks.html: 3.6.5.2. Data Entity/Business Function Matrix

blocks.text_en:
The purpose of the Data Entity/Business Function matrix is to depict the relationship between data entities and business functions within the
enterprise. Business functions are supported by business services with
explicitly defined boundaries and will be supported and realized by business processes. The mapping of the Data Entity-Business Function relationship enables the following to take place:
blocks.html: The purpose of the Data Entity/Business Function matrix is to depict the relationship between data entities and business functions within the enterprise. Business functions are supported by business services with explicitly defined boundaries and will be supported and realized by business processes. The mapping of the Data Entity-Business Function relationship enables the following to take place:

blocks.text_en:
Assign ownership of data entities to organizations Understand the data and information exchange requirements business
services Support the gap analysis and determine whether any data entities are
missing and need to be created Define application of origin, application of record, and application
of reference for data entities Enable development of data governance programs across the enterprise
(establish data steward, develop data standards pertinent to the
business function, etc.)
blocks.html:
• Assign ownership of data entities to organizations

  • Understand the data and information exchange requirements business services

  • Support the gap analysis and determine whether any data entities are missing and need to be created

  • Define application of origin, application of record, and application of reference for data entities

  • Enable development of data governance programs across the enterprise (establish data steward, develop data standards pertinent to the business function, etc.)

The Data Entity/Business Function matrix shows the following entities
and relationships:
blocks.html: The Data Entity/Business Function matrix shows the following entities and relationships:

  • Business Function

blocks.text_en: 3.6.5.3. Application/Data Matrix
blocks.html: 3.6.5.3. Application/Data Matrix

blocks.text_en:
The purpose of the Application/Data matrix is to depict the relationship
between applications (i.e., application components) and the data
entities that are accessed and updated by them.
blocks.html: The purpose of the Application/Data matrix is to depict the relationship between applications (i.e., application components) and the data entities that are accessed and updated by them.

blocks.text_en:
Applications will create, read, update, and delete specific data
entities that are associated with them. For example, a Customer
Relationship Management (CRM) application will create, read, update, and
delete customer entity information.
blocks.html: Applications will create, read, update, and delete specific data entities that are associated with them. For example, a Customer Relationship Management (CRM) application will create, read, update, and delete customer entity information.

blocks.text_en:
The data entities in a package/packaged services environment can be
classified as master data, reference data, transactional data, content
data, and historical data. Applications that operate on the data
entities include transactional applications, information management
applications, and business warehouse applications.
blocks.html: The data entities in a package/packaged services environment can be classified as master data, reference data, transactional data, content data, and historical data. Applications that operate on the data entities include transactional applications, information management applications, and business warehouse applications.

blocks.text_en:
The mapping of the Application Component-Data Entity relationship is an
important step as it enables the following to take place:
blocks.html: The mapping of the Application Component-Data Entity relationship is an important step as it enables the following to take place:

blocks.text_en:
Assign access of data to specific applications in the organization Understand the degree of data duplication within different
applications, and the scale of the data lifecycle Understand where the same data is updated by different applications Support the gap analysis and determine whether any of the applications
are missing and as a result need to be created
blocks.html:
• Assign access of data to specific applications in the organization

  • Understand the degree of data duplication within different applications, and the scale of the data lifecycle

  • Understand where the same data is updated by different applications

  • Support the gap analysis and determine whether any of the applications are missing and as a result need to be created

blocks.text_en:
The Application/Data matrix is a two-dimensional table with Logical
Application Component on one axis and Data Entity on the other axis.
blocks.html: The Application/Data matrix is a two-dimensional table with Logical Application Component on one axis and Data Entity on the other axis.

blocks.text_en: 3.6.5.4. Conceptual Data Diagram
blocks.html: 3.6.5.4. Conceptual Data Diagram

blocks.text_en: The key purpose of the Conceptual Data diagram is to depict the relationships between critical data entities within the enterprise. This diagram is developed to address the concerns of business stakeholders.
blocks.html: The key purpose of the Conceptual Data diagram is to depict the relationships between critical data entities within the enterprise. This diagram is developed to address the concerns of business stakeholders.

blocks.text_en: Techniques used include:
blocks.html: Techniques used include:
